There Will Be Blood

 

This is about as good as it gets for Big Oil.

 

The two U.S. energy supermajors, ExxonMobil and Chevron, are each set to report one of their most profitable quarters ever on Friday morning. Wars in Iran and Ukraine have put integrated producers like them—those that both pump and refine crude—in a sweet spot that seemingly refuses to end.

 

But investors know it will, because it always does for commodities. High prices encourage consumers to conserve resources and seek alternatives, while for producers they motivate more investment to capture those extraordinary profits.

 

There seems to be a fairly close connection between how much their market value has increased and how much expectations for free cash flow per share have risen since the attack on Iran eight months ago. That’s the money left over to reward shareholders.

 

Another booming but notoriously cyclical sector, computer memory, doesn’t look as grounded. There are two explanations for that. 

 

One is that the AI boom will be so big and long-lasting that it’ll extend years beyond analysts’ forecast horizon. The other explanation is that investors have gotten ahead of themselves.

 

The gains are on an entirely different scale than energy. Exxon and Chevron shares are up by 19% and 23%, respectively, since fighting began in Iran. Those of Micron and Sandisk are up about 1,000% and 3,700% since early 2025. The computer memory companies’ shares have appreciated two-and-a-half times as much as the cumulative increase in analysts’ consensus free-cash-flow expectations compiled by FactSet through fiscal year 2028.

 

Their business has seen booms and busts just like energy, but the collective memories of investors bidding their shares up today might be shorter. Each Micron share has changed hands six times as frequently as one of Exxon so far this year.

 

Popular new funds have specifically targeted computer memory as profits and stock prices soared. One launched in April by Roundhill became the fastest-growing ETF of all time.

 

Oil and chips are like apples and oranges, but money is money. And, if one sector deserves some benefit of the doubt on valuation, it’s probably energy. A refinery in Texas, oil field in Guyana or LNG terminal in Louisiana have become a bit more valuable than before the Strait of Hormuz was blocked since they face less risk of disruption.

 

With China pouring resources into semiconductors to achieve self-sufficiency, the political winds blow the other way for the memory business. Beijing’s race to catch up in quality and quantity could one day flood the market in ways Western companies wouldn’t consider rational.

 

What’s more, information technology evolves more quickly than hydrocarbons to get around shortages. You might be driving a 10-year old car, but you aren’t using a smartphone that old.

 

Investors in oil supermajors may not have much more upside ahead of them. They’ll probably face less downside when today’s profit bonanza ends, though.

↗️ Microsoft: The technology giant climbed 3% premarket after it reported accelerating growth in its cloud-computing unit, relieving investors’ worries about demand for its AI infrastructure services.

 

↘️ Samsung Electronics: The South Korean chip maker fell 4% after its net profit fell short of analysts’ expectations, even as it reported its fourth consecutive quarter of record earnings.

 

↗️ Shell: The oil major climbed nearly 3% in London trading after it reported bumper profits from its refining business amid the global fuel crunch.

 

↗️ Chipotle Mexican Grill: The burrito chain rose more than 6% premarket after it reported higher quarterly revenue and a gain in comparable-restaurant sales.

 

↗️ eBay: The e-commerce platform is up more than 6% in premarket trading after strength in its collectibles business pushed third-quarter profit and revenue above Wall Street’s expectations.

 

🔎 Amazon.com: The e-commerce and cloud-computing giant will be the next Big Tech name to report earnings, after today’s closing bell. Other companies reporting today include Intel.

 
 
 

One Big Chart

 
 
 
 

Oil exports from the Persian Gulf have rebounded significantly, at times returning to and even surpassing their prewar volumes. But prices for the global benchmark Brent have once again climbed to around $110 a barrel, a level last seen in late April when exports were about half of what they are now. The price rally reflects fears of renewed escalation, dwindling oil stockpiles and a makeshift shipping system that remains dangerous and expensive to operate.

• Google parent Alphabet is getting hit hard in early trading after disclosing disappointing search results. It still has arrows in its quiver to compete. (WSJ)

• A $30 billion spending spree is set to give the federal government stakes in chip makers, miners and more. (WSJ)

 

• Alphabet’s cloud business looked good. Its Google search business didn’t. (Barron’s)
